# Book I, Proposition 4

*Side, angle, side*

> If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend.

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/04.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.4, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB to DE and AC to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF.

I say that the base BC is also equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC will be equal to the triangle DEF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend, that is, the angle ABC to the angle DEF, and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.

For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF,

and if the point A be placed on the point D

and the straight line AB on DE,

then the point B will also coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE.

Again, AB coinciding with DE,

the straight line AC will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF;

hence the point C will also coincide with the point F, because AC is again equal to DF.

But B also coincided with E;

hence the base BC will coincide with the base EF.

[For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with the base EF, two straight lines will enclose a space: which is impossible.

Therefore the base BC will coincide with EF] and will be equal to it. [C.N. 4]

Thus the whole triangle ABC will coincide with the whole triangle DEF,

and will be equal to it.

And the remaining angles will also coincide with the remaining angles and will be equal to them,

the angle ABC to the angle DEF,

and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.

Therefore etc.

(Being) what it was required to prove.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop04.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop04.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- What Euclid sees in the figure but never says, when "the point B will also
coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE": a point `P` on the ray from `D`
through `E`, as far from `D` as `E` is, is `E` itself. This is Sir Henry
Savile's argument, which Heath reports (vol. 1, p. 250): otherwise `P` falls
short of `E` or beyond it, and either way the less would be equal to the
greater. -/
theorem Prop4.coincide {D E P : Point} (hP : OnRay P D E) (h : ‖D P‖ = ‖D E‖) :
    P = E := by
  obtain ⟨hDE, hPD, ⟨L, hD, hE, hPL⟩, hPDE⟩ := hP
  refine Classical.byContradiction fun (hPE : P ≠ E) => ?_
  rcases between_cases hPD.symm hPE hDE hD hPL hE with h' | h' | h'
  · /- `P` falls short of `E`: then `DE` is `DP` and `PE` together, and so
       greater than `DP`, which is equal to it. -/
    have hsum : ‖D P‖ + ‖P E‖ = ‖D P‖ := (len_add_of_between h').trans h.symm
    have hlt := CommonNotion5 (a := ‖D P‖) (len_pos hPE)
    rw [hsum] at hlt
    exact lt_irrefl _ hlt
  · /- `P` is on the far side of `D`, off the ray altogether. -/
    exact hPDE h'
  · /- `P` falls beyond `E`: then `DP` is `DE` and `EP` together, and so
       greater than `DE`, which is equal to it. -/
    have hsum : ‖D E‖ + ‖E P‖ = ‖D E‖ := (len_add_of_between h').trans h
    have hlt := CommonNotion5 (a := ‖D E‖) (len_pos hPE.symm)
    rw [hsum] at hlt
    exact lt_irrefl _ hlt

/-- What Euclid sees in the figure but never says, when "the straight line AC
will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF":
on one side of the straight line `DE`, only one ray from `D` makes a given
angle with `DE`. So a point `P` on the same side of `DE` as `F`, with the angle
`EDP` equal to the angle `EDF`, lies on the ray from `D` through `F`. -/
theorem Prop4.on_ray {D E F P : Point} {L : Line} (hDE : D ≠ E) (hDF : D ≠ F)
    (hD : OnLine D L) (hE : OnLine E L) (hPD : P ≠ D) (hPF : SameSide P F L)
    (h : ∠ E D P = ∠ E D F) : OnRay P D F := by
  obtain ⟨M, hD_M, hF_M⟩ := Postulate1 D F hDF
  have hP_L : ¬ OnLine P L := not_on_line_of_same_side hPF
  have hF_L : ¬ OnLine F L := not_on_line_of_same_side (same_side_symm hPF)
  have hLM : L ≠ M := fun e => hF_L (e ▸ hF_M)
  have hP_M : OnLine P M := by
    refine Classical.byContradiction fun hP_M => ?_
    /- Off the straight line `DF`, the point `P` makes some angle with `DF`
       (System E, Diagram-angle 1). -/
    have hFDP : 0 < ∠ F D P := Magnitude.pos_of_ne_zero fun h0 =>
      hP_M (same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero hDF hPD.symm hD_M hF_M h0).1
    by_cases hs : SameSide E P M
    · /- `P` lies within the angle `EDF`, so the angle `EDP` is a part of the
         angle `EDF` (Diagram-angle 2): the part would be equal to the whole. -/
      have hadd : ∠ E D F = ∠ E D P + ∠ P D F :=
        angle_add_of_inside hD hD_M hE hF_M hDE hDF hP_L hP_M hLM hs (same_side_symm hPF)
      rw [h, angle_symm hPD hDF.symm] at hadd
      have hlt := CommonNotion5 (a := ∠ E D F) hFDP
      rw [← hadd] at hlt
      exact lt_irrefl _ hlt
    · /- `F` lies within the angle `EDP` (Triple incidence 2), so the angle
         `EDF` is a part of the angle `EDP`: again the part would be equal to
         the whole. -/
      obtain ⟨N, hD_N, hP_N⟩ := Postulate1 D P hPD.symm
      have hEF_N : SameSide E F N :=
        triple_incidence2 hD hD_M hD_N hE hF_M hP_N (same_side_symm hPF) hs hP_M hDE.symm
      have hF_N : ¬ OnLine F N := fun hF_N =>
        hP_M (line_unique hDF hD_N hF_N hD_M hF_M ▸ hP_N)
      have hLN : L ≠ N := fun e => hP_L (e ▸ hP_N)
      have hadd : ∠ E D P = ∠ E D F + ∠ F D P :=
        angle_add_of_inside hD hD_N hE hP_N hDE hPD.symm hF_L hF_N hLN hEF_N hPF
      rw [h] at hadd
      have hlt := CommonNotion5 (a := ∠ E D F) hFDP
      rw [← hadd] at hlt
      exact lt_irrefl _ hlt
  /- And `P` is on `F`'s side of `D`, not beyond `D`: a point between `P` and
     `F` would put them on opposite sides of `DE` (Pasch 3). -/
  exact ⟨hDF, hPD, ⟨M, hD_M, hF_M, hP_M⟩, fun hb => pasch3 hb hD hPF⟩

/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles
contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the
triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining
angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. -/
theorem Prop4 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hA : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F) :
    ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ ∧ △ A B C = △ D E F ∧ ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F ∧ ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF
  -- respectively, namely AB to DE and AC to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF.
  have hBA : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
  have hCA : C ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₃.symm
  have hCB : C ≠ B := hABC.ne₂₃.symm
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hDEF.ne₁₂
  have hDF : D ≠ F := hDEF.ne₁₃
  have hFE : F ≠ E := hDEF.ne₂₃.symm
  -- I say that the base BC is also equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC will be equal to the
  -- triangle DEF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively,
  -- namely those which the equal sides subtend, that is, the angle ABC to the angle DEF, and
  -- the angle ACB to the angle DFE.
  -- For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF,
  /- Euclid lays the triangle along the straight line DE, on the side where F
     is. Lean needs that line by name, and F off it. -/
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE
  have hF_DE : ¬ OnLine F DE := fun hF => hDEF ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE, hF⟩
  -- and if the point A be placed on the point D
  -- and the straight line AB on DE,
  /- This is superposition, the one rule that moves a figure (System E §3.7, in
     LeanEuclid's form). The triangle ABC, laid down with A on D, becomes the
     triangle DB'C': B' is on the ray from D through E, C' is on the same side
     of DE as F, and every side and angle is kept. -/
  obtain ⟨B', C', hB'_DE, hB'_ray, hC'_side, hDB', hB'C', hC'D, hB'DC', hDC'B', hC'B'D⟩ :=
    superposition hABC hD_DE hE_DE hDE hF_DE
  have hB'D : B' ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq ((len_symm B' D).trans hDB') hBA.symm
  have hC'D' : C' ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq hC'D hCA
  have hB'C'' : B' ≠ C' := ne_of_len_eq hB'C' hCB.symm
  -- then the point B will also coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE.
  have hDB'_DE : ‖D B'‖ = ‖D E‖ := hDB'.trans hAB
  have hB'E : B' = E :=
    Prop4.coincide ⟨hDE, hB'D, ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE, hB'_DE⟩, hB'_ray⟩ hDB'_DE
  -- Again, AB coinciding with DE,
  have hEDC' : ∠ E D C' = ∠ B' D C' := CommonNotion4.angle hB'E.symm rfl rfl
  -- the straight line AC will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the
  -- angle EDF;
  have hEDC'_EDF : ∠ E D C' = ∠ E D F := hEDC'.trans (hB'DC'.trans hA)
  have hC'_ray : OnRay C' D F := Prop4.on_ray hDE hDF hD_DE hE_DE hC'D' hC'_side hEDC'_EDF
  -- hence the point C will also coincide with the point F, because AC is again equal to DF.
  have hDC'_DF : ‖D C'‖ = ‖D F‖ :=
    (len_symm D C').trans (hC'D.trans ((len_symm C A).trans hAC))
  have hC'F : C' = F := Prop4.coincide hC'_ray hDC'_DF
  -- But B also coincided with E;
  -- hence the base BC will coincide with the base EF.
  -- [For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with the base
  -- EF, two straight lines will enclose a space: which is impossible.
  /- Heiberg brackets this passage as an early scholium. Lean has no need of
     it: a finite straight line is fixed by its ends, so once B' is E and C'
     is F, the base B'C' simply is EF. -/
  -- Therefore the base BC will coincide with EF] and will be equal to it. [C.N. 4]
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ := hB'C'.symm.trans (CommonNotion4 hB'E hC'F)
  -- Thus the whole triangle ABC will coincide with the whole triangle DEF,
  have hcoincide : △ D B' C' = △ D E F := CommonNotion4.triangle rfl hB'E hC'F
  -- and will be equal to it.
  /- Being moved does not change the triangle: DB'C' has the same sides and
     angles as ABC, so the same area (System E, Metric 9). -/
  have hmoved : △ A B C = △ D B' C' :=
    area_congruent hDB'.symm hB'C'.symm hC'D.symm
      ((angle_symm hBA.symm hCB).trans (hC'B'D.symm.trans (angle_symm hB'C''.symm hB'D.symm)))
      ((angle_symm hCB.symm hCA.symm).trans (hDC'B'.symm.trans (angle_symm hC'D'.symm hB'C'')))
      ((angle_symm hCA hBA).trans (hB'DC'.symm.trans (angle_symm hB'D hC'D')))
  have harea : △ A B C = △ D E F := hmoved.trans hcoincide
  -- And the remaining angles will also coincide with the remaining angles and will be equal to
  -- them,
  -- the angle ABC to the angle DEF,
  have hB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F :=
    (angle_symm hBA.symm hCB).trans
      (hC'B'D.symm.trans ((CommonNotion4.angle hC'F hB'E rfl).trans (angle_symm hFE hDE)))
  -- and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.
  have hC : ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E := hDC'B'.symm.trans (CommonNotion4.angle rfl hC'F hB'E)
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hBC, harea, hB, hC⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to prove.
```

- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23): The line `AB` is the line `BA`. (Metric 3)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L49): If the angle `BAC` is nothing, `C` lies on the ray from `A` through `B`. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L29): **Superposition.** The triangle `ABC` can be applied to the straight line `L` with `A` on `D`, `B` on the ray from `D` through `G`, and `C` on the side of `L` where `H` is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L25): Adding is commutative. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L44): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L28): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L31): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L38): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L41): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

## Mishnah

**Picking up a triangle.** Euclid proves side–angle–side by lifting the triangle ABC and laying it down on DEF, and Heath thinks he did it unwillingly: "Euclid obviously used the method of superposition with reluctance" (vol. 1, p. 249). Jacques Peletier (Peletarius) objected as early as 1557 that if figures could be moved about, "the whole of geometry would be full of such proofs", and ended his note: *cogitabimusque figuras figuris superponere, Mechanicum quippiam esse: intelligere vero, id demum esse Mathematicum*, laying figures on figures is mechanical, understanding is mathematics. Bertrand Russell thought Euclid "would have done better to assume I. 4 as an axiom, as is practically done by Hilbert" (both reported by Heath, vol. 1, p. 249); Hilbert takes the equality of the remaining angles as an axiom and proves the equality of the bases (vol. 1, p. 250). Michael Beeson, Julien Narboux and Freek Wiedijk, checking Book I in Coq and HOL Light, derive I.4 from their five-line axiom, which comes from Tarski's geometry. Here superposition is one named rule, [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean): the rule of §3.7 of Avigad, Dean and Mumma's System E, in the combined form LeanEuclid gives it. The certificate lets only I.4 and I.8 cite it.

**Where B falls.** Heath points to something "most editors seem to have failed to observe": at the very start Euclid assumes that "if A be placed on D, and AB on DE, the point B will coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE. That is, the converse of Common Notion 4 is assumed for straight lines" (vol. 1, p. 250). Sir Henry Savile saw the gap and closed it: "let B fall somewhere short of E or beyond E; and in either case it will follow that the less is equal to the greater, which is impossible" (vol. 1, p. 250). That is the Lean lemma `Prop4.coincide`, step for step: of three points on a straight line one lies between the other two (System E, Between rule 6), the pieces add up to the whole (Diagram-segment rule 1), and the whole is greater than the part (Common Notion 5). Heath's further worry, why B should land on DE at all, is answered by the superposition rule itself, which lays AB along the ray from D through E.

**Where AC falls.** Next, AC "will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF." This is a second unspoken fact: on one side of DE, only one ray from D makes a given angle with DE. Heath lists the matching existence statement among the things Euclid "really assumes": "On either side of the ray DE there is a ray DF such that the angle EDF is equal to the angle BAC" (vol. 1, p. 250). Lean proves the uniqueness as `Prop4.on_ray`. If the point C′ where C lands were off DF, then either C′ would lie within the angle EDF or F within the angle EDC′ (Triple-incidence rule 2 says which), and either way an angle would be part of an angle equal to it (Diagram-angle rules 1 and 2, with Common Notion 5 again). Pasch rule 3 puts C′ on F's side of D rather than behind it.

**The words in brackets.** Heiberg brackets the sentence about two straight lines enclosing a space, because the Arabic text of an-Nairīzī gives it only after the conclusion, "which shows that they constitute a scholium only". It was added, Heath says, to explain "an inference which really follows from the definition of a straight line and Post. 1" (vol. 1, p. 249). Lean doesn't need it either: a length is the length between two points, so once B′ is E and C′ is F the base B′C′ simply is EF, and Common Notion 4 says no more than that.

**Equal triangles.** The superposition rule promises that every side and angle is kept, but it says nothing about area. That the triangle laid down has the area of ABC is System E's Metric rule 9, [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean): triangles that agree in all their sides and angles are equal. After that, Common Notion 4 finishes the job, as Euclid says. And because Euclid lays the triangle along DE, Lean needs that straight line by name, which puts Postulate 1 on the certificate.

**The modern way.** With vectors, BC² = AB² + AC² − 2·AB·AC·cos A, so the two sides and the angle between them fix the base, and also the area, ½·AB·AC·sin A. Superposition itself is a rigid motion: in the complex plane, z ↦ az + b or z ↦ a z̄ + b with |a| = 1, carrying A to D, B to E and C to F.
